 TRANSMISSION LINE IN BELL,                    §
 BURNET, CONCHO, CORYELL,                      §
 LAMPASAS, LLANO, MASON,                       §

 MILLS, SAN SABA, SCHLEICHER,                  §

 REPLIES TO EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION BY CHEROKEE
  CREEK PARTNERS, BONNIE HELENE MCANELLY, INDIVIDUALLY AND AS
   TRUSTEE OF THE 2025 HOMESTEAD TRUST AND THE BONNIE HELENE
  MCANELLY 2023 TRUST (“CHEROKEE CREEK ALIGNED INTERVENORS”)

        COMES NOW, Cherokee Creek Partners, Bonnie Helene McAnelly, Individually and as

Trustee of the 2025 Homestead Trust and the Bonnie Helene McAnelly 2023 Trust (“Cherokee

Creek Aligned Intervenors”) and file their Reply to the Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision

(“PFD”) filed by other parties.

   I.      INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT

        Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors join the many parties who urge the Commission to

adopt the Administrative Law Judges’ (“ALJs”) primary recommendation and deny the

Application. The Exceptions confirm what the record already showed: this is a deeply contested

routing proceeding in which no Focus Route commands consensus. More importantly, the routing

decisions emerged without the full development and analysis of the record necessary to

meaningfully distinguish among the competing routes. The emphasis on the need for the project
 and the notice defect diverted attention from the central routing inquiry and left important route-

specific evidence and considerations insufficiently examined.

        These replies are offered solely in the alternative, in the event the Commission certifies a

route notwithstanding denial on other grounds. Should the Commission reach route selection, the

exceptions — read together — reinforce that Route Cherokee Creek G (“Route CCG”) is the route

that best balances the statutory and rule criteria of PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 Texas Administrative

Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B). No single factor controls that balance for any of the Focus Routes. Three

themes run through the other parties’ Exceptions, and each favors Route CCG:

        The southern crossing is the right crossing, but Route CCG reaches it without

endangering a school. Save the Lampasas, the Link N3 Opposition Landowners, and the G-9 and

G-13 Landowners all urge the Commission to select Route 296, a Southern Corridor route, over

the ALJs’ recommended Route 894. They are correct that a southern Colorado River crossing is

superior. But each concedes that Route 296, as filed, places a transmission line within 500 feet of

the newly built Florence Elementary School, and each landowner group is reduced promising a

future “minor adjustment” of Link F34 or a patchwork “Route 296 Option A” to cure that defect.

Route CCG needs no such cure: it captures the southern-crossing advantages while avoiding the

school entirely.

        Paralleling existing infrastructure provides a more meaningful measure of paralleling

than following “apparent property lines.” The Link N3 Opposition Landowners, the G-9 and G-

13 Landowners, Staten Creek Ranch, and the Brady Creek Intervenors all attack Route 894’s

paralleling figure as an artifact of unreliable “apparent property boundaries” rather than hard,

 verifiable compatible infrastructure. That criticism is well taken, and Route CCG parallels roughly

three times more existing transmission-line right-of-way and roads/highways than Route 894. 1

          The lone exception opposing Route CCG raises nothing new. The M31, M32, and M33

Opposition Landowners oppose Route CCG on cost, length, habitable-structure count, and a

“single point of failure” at the San Saba River. 2 In short, the M31, M32, and M33 Opposition

Landowners have dressed up marginal numerical gaps as fatal flaws. Each ground was answered

in the record and is answered again below.


    II.      THE COMMISSION SHOULD ADOPT THE ALJS’                                          PRIMARY
             RECCOMENDATION AND DENY THE APPLICATION

          The ALJs correctly concluded that the Applicants did not carry their burden of

demonstrating that the transmission lines comprising Import Path 2 are needed, and the

Commission should adopt that conclusion. The burden of proving that a proposed facility is

necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public under PURA §

37.056(a) rests on the Applicants, and the PFD found they did not meet it.

          Commission Staff excepts, arguing that ERCOT’s recommendation that the 765-kV import

paths are needed is entitled to “great weight” and that the PFD erred in declining to defer to it.3

Great weight, however, is not conclusive weight, and it cannot substitute for the proof the record

lacks. The PFD found that the preponderance of the evidence outweighed ERCOT’s

recommendation and that the Applicants failed to demonstrate need.

         The record supports that finding, because the need case rested on load projections shown

to be overstated and untested:

    -   The Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”) load forecast was built on the S&P Global
        study and on officer-letter attestations - 55% of the non-oil-and-gas load was officer-letter
        confirmed, 6% unconfirmed, and 6% data centers — and was never retested against
        ERCOT’s later, more conservative load-forecasting methodology. 4

    -   After the PBRP was approved, ERCOT adopted an adjusted methodology that discounted
        officer-letter-confirmed load to 55.4% and data-center load to 49.8% of forecasted
        megawatts, based on historical realization rates. 5 Applying that methodology to the
        PBRP’s non-oil-and-gas projections would reduce the forecasted load by at least 3,571
        MW — undermining the need for Import Path 2, whose safe loading limit is 5,270 MW. 6

    -   The S&P Global study’s central premise — that Permian Basin producers had to electrify
        to reduce their absolute greenhouse-gas emissions — was disproven by S&P Global’s own
        later analysis, which showed emissions fell approximately 20% between 2022 and 2025
        even as production rose, rendering the projected load overstated and outdated. 7

    -   The Applicants did not evaluate any alternatives to the projects making up Import Path 2. 8

    On this record, the Applicants failed to show that the PBRP’s projected loads establish a need

for the Bell County East-to-Big Hill and Big Hill-to-Sand Lake Projects that together comprise

Import Path 2. Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors respectfully urge the Commission to adopt the

ALJs’ recommendation and deny the Application for lack of demonstrated need. The replies that

follow are presented solely in the alternative.

     III.      IF A ROUTE IS SELECTED, THE EXCEPTIONS CONFIRM THAT ROUTE
              CCG BEST BALANCES THE STATUTORY CRITERIA

              a. Route CCG is the superior southern route: it secures the advantages of Route
                 296 proponents seek, while avoiding Florence Elementary School entirely.

           Save the Lampasas, the Link N3 Opposition Landowners, and the G-9 and G-13

Landowners each urge the Commission to reject Route 894 in favor of the Southern Corridor’s

Route 296. Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors agree with these parties on the decisive point: a

southern Colorado River crossing that uses the pre-existing infrastructure corridor is

environmentally superior to Route 894’s crossing near the two state parks. Where these parties err

is in tying that advantage to Route 296, a route that carries a serious community-values liability

Route CCG does not.

           Route 296, as filed, relies on Link F34, which passes within 500 feet of Florence

Elementary School — a brand-new facility serving more than 500 students daily. 9 Route 296 also

relies on Link G31, which runs near the actively expanding Matterhorn Compressor Station.10

Route CCG uses neither Link F34 nor Link G31, and therefore avoids both risks outright. 11 The

data confirm the point: Route CCG has zero schools within 500 feet of its centerline, while Route

296 has one. 12

           The Route 296 proponents do not deny this liability; they propose to engineer around it

after the fact. Save the Lampasas and the G-9 and G-13 Landowners ask the Commission to trust

that Link F34 can later be nudged more than 1,000 feet from the school, or that the Applicants will

 use “best efforts” to mitigate, or that the hybrid “Route 296 Option A” can be assembled from

Route 894’s eastern links to skip Link F34 altogether. 13 Those proposals prove Route CCG’s point

rather than rebut it. A route that must be re-drawn on an individual property to protect a school is

inferior to a route designed from the outset to avoid the school across the full corridor. Route CCG

is that route. It does not ask the Commission to certify a defect on the promise of a later fix; it

eliminates the defect by design. 14

        Route CCG also follows the best path through the eastern portion of the study area. The

Route 296 proponents’ own fallback — “Route 296 Option A” — concedes as much: it abandons

Route 296’s eastern links and adopts an eastern alignment precisely to avoid Florence

Elementary. 15 Route CCG achieves that objective directly, retaining the favorable portions of the

Focus Routes in the east while departing only where the record shows a measurable

improvement. 16 The Link N3 Opposition Landowners fault the PFD for over-focusing on the

eastern half of the study area at the expense of the west; Route CCG answers that concern by

performing well across the entire corridor rather than trading east against west. 17

             b. The Exceptions confirm the Route CCG best protects private property owners
                because it parallels real compatible infrastructure, not “apparent property
                lines.”

         A striking point of agreement runs through the exceptions of the Link N3 Opposition

Landowners, the G-9 and G-13 Landowners, Staten Creek Ranch, and the Brady Creek

Intervenors: Route 894’s headline paralleling advantage is an illusion built on “apparent property

boundaries” rather than real, verifiable compatible infrastructure. The Brady Creek Intervenors put

it plainly — “apparent” boundaries are “often in fact NOT boundaries at all,” including section

lines, county lines, and old fence lines, and should be given far less weight than “hard” paralleling

of existing transmission lines and roadways, which “matches infrastructure with infrastructure and

is inherently and objectively verifiable.” 18 Commission Rule 16 Texas Administrative Code §

25.101(b)(3)(B)(iii) requires paralleling of “property lines,” not “apparent property lines,” and

Staff’s own witness acknowledged that apparent-property-boundary measures are “less reliable

than existing compatible infrastructure.” 19

        This shared criticism is the strongest argument in the record for Route CCG. When

paralleling is measured by real infrastructure, Route CCG outperforms Route 894 decisively:

Route CCG parallels 14.02 miles of existing transmission line right-of-way — roughly two-and-

a-half times Route 894’s 5.66 miles — and 15.41 miles of public roads and highways, more than

triple Route 894’s 4.45 miles. 20 While Route 392 performs better than Route CCG in these

categories as well, it does so with a significantly more structure count. 21

        That distinction is not academic; it is the difference between protecting private property

and fragmenting it. Paralleling existing corridors holistically avoids the bisection of private tracts

 across the entire route. Save the Lampasas explains why individual-property fixes cannot

substitute: Route 894 bisects more than ten miles of properties on a diagonal along Links G51 and

G52, and that bisection “could not be effectively mitigated by siting modification to move the line

along property lines, because to do so, would require more than dozens of turning structures in the

line.” 22 These harms are the predictable consequence of routing along apparent property

boundaries instead of real corridors. Route CCG, by paralleling actual transmission and road

corridors, protects landowners at the design stage — where bisection is genuinely avoidable —

rather than promising piecemeal adjustments that the record shows are often impossible and

costly. 23

               c. Commission Staff’s case for Route 487 confirms that Route CCG better
                  protects the two state parks.

           Commission Staff excepts in favor of Route 487, emphasizing its shorter length, lower

cost, and strong compatible infrastructure paralleling. Staff’s paralleling argument, however, only

reinforces the criticism of “apparent property boundary” measurement discussed above, and it

cannot rehabilitate Route 487’s critical weakness: its proximity to Colorado Bend State Park. Staff

concedes that Route 487 sits just 0.02 miles from Colorado Bend State Park. 24 The record shows

Route 487 carries 4.25 miles of right-of-way within the foreground visual zone of parks and

recreational areas — by far the worst of any route in contention — and is the only Focus Route

with a park or recreational area within 1,000 feet of its centerline. 25 Route CCG, by contrast,

 registers zero miles within that foreground visual zone, and — unlike Route 894 — places no state-

park acreage within the critical 0.5-to-1-mile band, where Route 894 places 442.65 acres. 26

        Whether the Commission selects Route 487 or Route 894, the result is the same: large high-

voltage transmission towers erected within a mile of two of Texas’s significant state parks,

permanently marring the natural beauty these public lands were set aside to protect. Both Route

487 and Route 894 would inflict severe, unavoidable harm on Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge

State Parks—roughly 8,500 acres of unspoiled Hill Country straddling the Colorado River,

drawing tens of thousands of visitors each year. 27 PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(B) requires the

Commission to weigh impacts on parks and recreational areas, and on that criterion, Route CCG

is the strongest route in contention while carefully weighing the other factors. Staff’s request that

park impacts be treated as “not a distinguishing factor” would read a statutory criterion out of the

analysis and should be rejected. 28

            d. The Northern Corridor Exceptions Do Not Displace Route CCG, but Route
               410 Provides the Best Northern Alternative.

        Staten Creek Ranch and the Brady Creek Intervenors urge selection of Northern Corridor

Routes 392 or 410. Their central premise — that a river crossing should be made alongside existing

infrastructure rather than through undisturbed land — is one Route CCG shares and satisfies at

both major river crossings on the Colorado and San Saba. But the Northern Corridor routes

purchase their transmission-paralleling advantage at a steep price. Route 392 is the longest and

sites crossed — eight times Route CCG’s two. 29

        Notably, Staten Creek Ranch states that it is “unopposed” to the Southern Corridor routes,

including Route CCG, recognizing that they “mitigate the extreme qualitative downsides of the

Central Corridor routes while performing similarly on a quantitative basis.” 30 Route CCG delivers

the environmental and paralleling objectives the Northern Corridor proponents seek, without

Route 392’s length, cost, habitable-structure, and cultural-resource burdens.

        If the Commission proceeds with a Northern Corridor route, it should select Route 410. It

crosses the Colorado River at Link U3, paralleling the existing LCRA 138-kV line rather than

opening a new crossing near Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks, while impacting only

98 habitable structures within 500 feet of centerline. 31 Its modest cost premium falls within the

contingency range the Staff’s witness confirmed as not a distinguishing factor. 32 Route 410’s data

is already in the record, notwithstanding the severe time constraints at hearing, including the denial

of separate cross-examination time, that foreclosed fuller development of the routing testimony. 33

summary dismissal of Route 410 (similarly to Route CCG) which the PFD rejected without

meaningful analysis or consideration of their merits. Route selection is not a popularity contest

among intervenors. PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101 require the route that best moderates

             e. The M31, M32, and M33 Opposition Landowners’ objections to Route CCG
                were answered in the record and do not withstand scrutiny.

        The M31, M32, and M33 Opposition Landowners are the only party to except in opposition

to Route CCG. Their four objections – length, cost, habitable structures, and a San Saba “single

point of failure” – do not distinguish Route CCG from the routes those same landowners are willing

to accept.

        Route CCG’s additional length and its approximately $40 million cost premium (roughly

2.4% above the Focus Routes) are neither inefficiency nor accident; every added mile reflects two

deliberate, responsive routing choices: crossing the Colorado River at Links J31–J32 alongside an

existing pipeline corridor and farther from Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks, and

crossing the San Saba River at Link L4 alongside an existing AEP 138-kV transmission line. 34

The ALJs themselves found that cost “was not a distinguishing factor” because the routes fall

within a relatively tight range, and Route CCG’s premium sits comfortably within the Joint

Applicants’ own 10-to-15% engineering contingency. 35 Route length is not itself a statutory

criterion, and it cannot override the park and environmental advantages those crossings produce.

        Route CCG has 105 habitable structures within 500 feet of its centerline — identical to

Route 296, and thirty-one fewer than Route 392. 36The twenty-structure gap against Route 894 and

the nine-structure gap against Route 487 both fall within a single standard deviation

        The resiliency objection, placing the project beside the existing AEP line at the San Saba

River crossing creates a single point of failure is speculative and unsupported. It originates in the

testimony of former Commissioner McAdams, who is not an engineer, performed no engineering

or probability analysis, and conceded only that simultaneous failure “could happen.” 40 By

contrast, LCRA TSC’s engineering witness testified that the Applicants’ foundation-design criteria

“significantly avoid the impacts of severe flooding,” and that structures of the type proposed here

“experienced no discernible damage” during the catastrophic July 2025 floods. 41 In any event,

flooding is not a distinguishing factor: the San Saba and Colorado Rivers must be crossed

regardless of route, and flood concerns were raised against every San Saba crossing in the study

area. 42 Crossing alongside existing transmission infrastructure is exactly what the paralleling

criteria and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department recommend, not a defect. 43

                                IV.     CONCLUSION AND PRAYER

        The exceptions, taken together, undermine the ALJs’ alternative recommendation of Route

894 and reinforce the case for Route CCG. The parties advocating Route 296 confirm the

superiority of a southern crossing while conceding a school-proximity defect that Route CCG

avoids by design. The parties attacking Route 894’s paralleling confirm that "apparent property

boundaries" supply an unreliable metric and that real compatible-infrastructure paralleling, at

which Route CCG performs very well, protects landowners from bisection. Staff’s advocacy for

Route 487 highlights that route’s unmatched park proximity, a harm Route CCG avoids. And the

sole exception opposing Route CCG repeats objections the record has already answered.

        Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors respectfully request that the Commission adopt the

ALJs’ primary recommendation and deny the Application. In the alternative, should the

Commission certify a route, Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors request that the Commission

approve Route CCG as the route that best balances the criteria of PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 Texas

Administrative Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B), and grant such other relief to which they may be entitled.
